spans.content: Original Software Publication
ClusterChoice: a web-based tool for interpretable clustering and algorithm
comparison in bibliometric networks
Tsair-Wei Chien <sup>a</sup>, Lifan Chen <sup>b,*</sup>, Willy Chou <sup>c,d,**</sup>
<sup>a</sup> Department of Medical Research, Chi Mei Medical Center, Tainan, Taiwan
<sup>b</sup> Department of Nursing, An Nan Hospital, China Medical University, Tainan, Taiwan
<sup>c</sup> Department of Leisure and Sports Management, CTBC University, Tainan, Taiwan
<sup>d</sup> Department of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, Chi-Mei Hospital, Liouying, Tainan, Taiwan
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
ClusterChoice
Bibliometrics
Cluster analysis
FLCA
Network visualization
A B S T R A C T
Cluster analysis is widely used in bibliometric research, but dense networks often reduce readability, and
clustering algorithms or quality indicators are frequently underreported. This study introduces ClusterChoice, a
web-based R Shiny application for selecting interpretable clustering structures in bibliometric networks. The
software accepts co-word occurrence, document–term matrix, and node–edge data, applies top-node filtering to
reduce computational burden, and compares 11 clustering algorithms using modularity Q, mean silhouette score,
ARI, and NMI. A SoftwareX bibliographic dataset was used to demonstrate practical utility. In the comparative
analysis of 76 nodes(i.e., with many singleton with SS=0), most conventional algorithms showed similar
modularity (Q = 0.65) but near-zero silhouette scores, indicating weak cohesion despite acceptable partitioning.
Components-based methods improved silhouette values to 0.60–0.62. In contrast, FLCA achieved the highest
modularity (Q = 0.80) and mean silhouette score (0.78), producing clearer leader–follower clusters. The SSplot
for the top 20 nodes across six clusters further showed positive silhouette values, supporting cluster stability. By
integrating top-node filtering, FLCA-based clustering, algorithm comparison, network visualization, SSplots,
Kano plots, and exportable reports, ClusterChoice provides a practical and reproducible tool for improving
bibliometric cluster selection and network-quality assessment.
• Compares 11 clustering algorithms for bibliometric network analysis.
• Uses top-node filtering to reduce dense co-word network complexity.
• Reports modularity, silhouette, ARI, and NMI with exportable visual outputs.

spans.content: Table 1
Pseudocode of the FLCA leader–follower clustering procedure.

spans.html:
StagePseudocode
InputNode table with name, value, optional value2; edge table with paired nodes and WCD; parameters: cluster_by, top_clusters = 5, base_per_cluster = 4, target_n = 20, min_size = 3, intra_delta = 2, inter_delta = 5.
OutputFinal node clusters, leader-follower edges, top-20 sampled nodes, modularity Q, and silhouette statistics.
1Normalize node names and numeric scores.
2Select active FLCA score: use value for maturity mode or value2 for influence mode.
3Sort nodes by descending active score and assign initial unique cluster IDs.
4Normalize edges into Leader, Follower, and WCD.
5For each edge, assign the higher-scored node as Leader and the lower-scored node as Follower.
6For each follower, retain only one strongest leader link using maximum WCD; break ties by leader score and leader rank.
7Identify true leaders as nodes with at least two followers; always retain the top-scored node as a leader.
8Iteratively merge each non-leader follower into its leader's cluster until no cluster assignment changes.
9Detect small clusters with fewer than min_size members and merge them upward through their leader connection.
10If only one cluster remains, split it into two rank-based subclusters to avoid a trivial one-cluster result.
11Renumber clusters sequentially according to the highest active score within each cluster.
12Apply major sampling: rank clusters by size and total active score.
13Select the top top_clusters clusters.
14From each selected cluster, take up to base_per_cluster highest-scored nodes.
15Fill remaining positions by round-robin sampling from selected clusters until target_n = 20 is reached.
16If still fewer than 20 nodes, fill by global active-score ranking.
17Rebuild the sampled edge set using only edges among selected top-20 nodes.
18Compute modularity Q for the final sampled clusters using weighted and unweighted undirected edges.
19Compute silhouette statistics using distance transformed from edge weight: stronger WCD indicates shorter distance.
20Apply intra-cluster and inter-cluster penalties for missing edges using intra_delta and inter_delta.
21Return final clusters, leader-follower relations, sampled top-20 network, modularity Q, and silhouette values.

lusterchoice/
1. Motivation and significance
Clustering is a fundamental task in network analysis and community
detection, aiming to partition nodes into meaningful groups based on
structural relationships. Widely used algorithms, such as Louvain,
Walktrap, Infomap, and label propagation, have been extensively
applied in bibliometrics and complex network studies due to their
computational efficiency and scalability [1–3]. However, these methods
primarily optimize global criteria, such as modularity or information
flow, and often overlook structural constraints required for interpretable
clustering results [4].
1.1. Research gaps
A key limitation of existing approaches is the absence of explicit
hierarchical organization within clusters [5]. In many real-world
networks—particularly
bibliometric
and
collaboration
networks—relationships naturally exhibit leader–follower dynamics,
where central nodes (leaders) organize or influence surrounding nodes
(followers) [6–12]. Conventional algorithms do not enforce such struc-
tures, often producing clusters with weak cohesion, fragmented group-
ings, or leaders lacking sufficient supporting members [13]. Moreover,
dense co-word or collaboration networks frequently contain excessive
nodes and edges, resulting in cluttered layouts that hinder interpretation
[14]. Empirical studies further show that some algorithms may achieve
acceptable modularity while yielding low or even negative silhouette
scores, indicating poor internal cohesion [7,9].
These issues are particularly critical in bibliometric analysis. Author
collaboration networks are widely used to examine how scientific
knowledge is generated and organized, where nodes represent authors
and edges capture co-authorship or intellectual relationships [15]. In
practice, such collaborations are rarely flat; instead, they often reflect
implicit hierarchies in which senior or highly productive researchers act
as leaders, while junior collaborators form follower groups [8,9,16].
Therefore, clustering methods should not only partition networks into
communities but also reveal interpretable internal structures that reflect
these hierarchical relationships.
However, traditional clustering algorithms do not guarantee that
clusters satisfy basic interpretability conditions, such as having a clear
leader, sufficient members, and coherent internal connections [6]. This
limitation may lead to misleading conclusions in bibliometric studies,
particularly when interpreting academic leadership, mentoring capac-
ity, or collaborative structures.
1.2. ClusterChoice and FLCA
To address these gaps, this study introduces ClusterChoice [17], a
web-based application designed to improve clustering interpretability
and efficiency in bibliometric networks. The system integrates (i) a
top-node filtering strategy to reduce network complexity before clus-
tering, (ii) a leader–follower-oriented clustering framework based on
Following Leader Clustering Algorithm (FLCA) [8,9,16], and (iii) a
comparative evaluation module across multiple algorithms using met-
rics such as modularity, silhouette score, ARI, and NMI [18,19]. By
combining computational reduction with structural constraints, Clus-
terChoice[17] enables users to identify clustering solutions that are both
quantitatively robust and visually interpretable.
1.3. Study aims
The objective of this study is to evaluate whether FLCA can produce
more coherent and interpretable clustering results than conventional
methods. Using bibliometric datasets, ClusterChoice compares multiple
clustering algorithms and examines their ability to reveal meaningful
collaboration structures while satisfying key clustering principles.
Through this approach, the study aims to provide a practical and
reproducible framework for selecting appropriate clustering methods in
bibliometric and network analysis.
2. Software description and methodology
ClusterChoise is a web-based bibliometric clustering and network
analysis application developed in R with a Shiny interface. It is designed
to transform co-word occurrence data or network-based inputs into
interpretable clustering structures while reducing computational burden
through an adaptive node-selection strategy. Unlike conventional clus-
tering tools that operate on full-scale networks, ClusterChoise in-
troduces a top-N node preselection mechanism (default: top 100
nodes by importance to reduce computation with many nodes and re-
lations) to improve efficiency without sacrificing interpretability.
The application integrates data preprocessing, network construction,
clustering comparison, and visualization into a unified workflow. It
supports multiple clustering algorithms, including FLCA (Table 1) and
benchmark methods, and provides evaluation metrics such as silhouette
score, modularity, and agreement indices (ARI, NMI) [18,19]. The sys-
tem outputs interpretable visualizations including co-word networks,
SSplots [12], and Sankey-style summaries [5], enabling users to assess
clustering quality and thematic structure in a reproducible environment.

Fig. 1. ClusterChoice Workflow with 5 modules.
Step 2: Node importance estimation and top-N selection
2.1. System architecture
ClusterChoise follows a structured five-step analytical pipeline:
1. Data acquisition and normalization
2. Node importance estimation and top-N selection
3. Co-word network construction
4. Clustering and comparative evaluation
5. Visualization and export
This architecture converts raw co-word occurrence data or
document-derived inputs into a reduced yet informative network rep
resentation, followed by clustering analysis and visual interpretation.
A key design principle is computational reduction before clus-
tering. Instead of constructing and analyzing a full high-dimensional
network, ClusterChoise first identifies the most informative nodes and
restricts downstream computation to this subset. This improves scal
ability and stability, particularly for large bibliometric datasets.
Step 1: Data acquisition and normalization
The system accepts multiple input formats, including:
• Co-word occurrence tables (long format: document × term)
• Wide document-term matrices
• Predefined node–edge network data
Uploaded data are parsed into a standardized internal representa-
tion. Text-based inputs are transformed into term-level structures, while
network inputs are normalized into node and edge tables with consistent
naming conventions (e.g., Leader, follower, WCD).
This step ensures compatibility across heterogeneous data sources
and prepares the dataset for subsequent node evaluation and filtering.
To reduce computational complexity, ClusterChoise applies a node
filtering strategy prior to network construction. Each node is
assigned an importance score based on occurrence frequency or
weighted connectivity (e.g., co-occurrence strength).
Nodes are then ranked in descending order, and only the top-N nodes
(default: 100) are retained:
\mathscr {V} _ {t o p} = v _ {1}, v _ {2}, \dots , v _ {1 0 0}, \text {where} v a l u e (v _ {i}) \geq v a l u e (v _ {i + 1}),\tag{1}
This step is critical because co-word networks scale quadratically
with the number of nodes. By limiting the node set before edge gener-
ation, the algorithm significantly reduces memory usage and computa-
tional time.
Importantly, this design preserves the core thematic structure of
the dataset, as high-frequency or high-impact terms typically dominate
semantic representation.
Step 3: Co-word network construction
After node selection, ClusterChoise constructs a weighted co-word
network based only on the filtered node set. Edges are generated using
co-occurrence relationships:
• In document-based data: two terms are linked if they co-occur within
the same unit (e.g., sentence or document)
• In matrix data: co-occurrence is derived via matrix multiplication
• In edge input: weights are directly used
The co-occurrence matrix is defined as:
C = X ^ {T} X\tag{2}
where X is the binary document-term matrix restricted to top-N nodes.

Clustering quality is evaluated using:
• Modularity (Q) for network partition strength
• Silhouette score (SS) for cluster cohesion and separation
• Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) and Normalized Mutual Information
(NMI) for agreement comparison with FLCA
This multi-metric framework allows users to compare clustering
outcomes across methods and identify the most interpretable structure.
Step 5: Visualization and export
ClusterChoise generates multiple visual outputs:
• Co-word network graphs (leader–follower structure)
• SSplots for cluster quality assessment
• Kano-style plots for algorithm comparison
• Sankey diagrams for flow-based interpretation
These visualizations transform clustering results into interpretable
insights, enabling users to understand thematic organization and cluster
reliability.
The export module provides:
• Node and edge tables
• Clustering results
• High-resolution Figures
This supports reproducibility and facilitates integration into aca-
demic manuscripts.

A central innovation of ClusterChoise is its pre-clustering reduc-
tion strategy, where node filtering is applied before network con
struction and clustering.
Compared to traditional approaches:
Conventional workflow:
full nodes → full edges → clustering
• ClusterChoise workflow:
top-N nodes → reduced edges → clustering

2.2. Computational optimization strategy
A central innovation of ClusterChoise is its pre-clustering reduc-
tion strategy, where node filtering is applied before network con
struction and clustering.
Compared to traditional approaches:
Conventional workflow:
full nodes → full edges → clustering
• ClusterChoise workflow:
top-N nodes → reduced edges → clustering

This shift reduces computational complexity from:
O \big (n ^ {2} \big) \to O \big (k ^ {2} \big), k \ll n,\tag{3}
where n is the original number of nodes and k is the selected subset.
This design is particularly effective for large bibliometric datasets,
where full co-word matrices can be computationally expensive and
visually cluttered.
2.3. Implementation layers
ClusterChoise consists of four layers:
1. Interface layer (Shiny) – user input, parameter selection,
visualization
2. Preprocessing layer – data parsing and normalization
3. Analytical engine – node filtering, network construction, clustering
4. Rendering layer – visualization and export
This modular design separates user interaction from computation,
ensuring both usability and reproducibility.
2.4. ARI and NMI as similarity measures for clustering algorithms
ARI and NMI measure how similar each clustering result is to the
reference clustering structure [9,10].
Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) evaluates whether pairs of nodes are
assigned consistently across two clustering methods. A value of 1.00
means perfect agreement, whereas values near 0 indicate random-level
agreement.
Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) measures how much in-
formation one clustering result shares with another. A value of 1.00 also
indicates complete consistency between two clustering solutions.
2.5. User workflow
From a user perspective, the workflow is shown below (Fig. 2):
1. Upload co-word or document data
2. Select analysis settings (e.g., node limit, clustering method)
3. Run analysis
4. Inspect network and clustering results
5. Export outputs
This streamlined pipeline enables efficient exploration of biblio-
metric structures while maintaining methodological rigor.

Upload CSV files, choosing Co-word occurrence, browsing the dataset

FLCA Process tab to inspect visual results.
Additionally, the interface supports FLCA parameter configuration,
maturity/influence modes, clustering-quality evaluation, and export-
able visual outputs including network dashboards, SSplots, Kano plots,
Sankey diagrams, and downloadable publication-ready figures.

3.4.1. To examine whether the study achieved its goals
This section evaluates whether ClusterChoice achieved its main
goals: reducing network complexity, improving cluster interpretability,
and supporting algorithm selection. The results were examined using
visual readability, leader–follower structure, modularity Q, silhouette
score, and comparative algorithm performance. This assessment con-
firms that the proposed FLCA workflow provides clearer and more
reliable clustering outputs than conventional network clustering
approaches.
4. Impact
Unlike traditional bibliometric tools such as CiteSpace [22], VOS
viewer [23], and bibliometrix [24], ClusterChoice[17] integrates
FLCA-based leader–follower clustering [8,9,16] with pre-analysis
filtering, cluster-quality evaluation, and publication-oriented visualiza-
tion within a unified browser-based workflow. Rather than focusing
solely on network generation, the framework emphasizes interpretable
cluster structures, standardized evaluation, and reproducible compari
son of multiple clustering algorithms [4,7,12].
The practical impact of the framework lies primarily in balancing
computational efficiency, structural interpretability, and reproduc
ibility. The proposed top-N node preselection strategy (default: top 100
nodes) substantially reduces computational burden in dense biblio
metric networks by limiting the number of pairwise node relationships
processed during clustering and visualization. This filtering mechanism
improves runtime stability and visual readability while preserving the
dominant thematic structure of the network [7]. However,
low-frequency nodes may still contain potentially meaningful semantic
information, and therefore the filtering strategy represents a tradeoff
between computational tractability and fine-grained thematic
completeness.
ClusterChoice [17] further incorporates a structure-aware FLCA
framework based on leader–follower assignment, maximum-association
filtering, and major-sampling stabilization [8–12,16]. Compared with
several conventional clustering methods evaluated in this study, FLCA
produced higher overall modularity
( Q \approx 0 . 8 0 )
together with substan-
tially improved weighted mean silhouette scores
( S S \approx 0 . 7 8 – 0 . 8 8 ) _ { \scriptscriptstyle ; }
indicating stronger global edge separation and improved node-level
compactness. In contrast, several conventional methods produced
acceptable modularity values but near-zero silhouette scores, reflecting
fragmented cluster structures with weak local cohesion. These findings
suggest that modularity alone may not sufficiently represent clustering
quality in highly fragmented bibliometric networks [4,7,12].
The integrated evaluation framework additionally combines modu-
larity (Q), silhouette score (SS), adjusted Rand index (ARI), and
normalized mutual information (NMI), enabling objective comparison
of clustering structures generated by different algorithms [4,12]. This
design improves methodological transparency and addresses the limited
reproducibility and inconsistent reporting frequently observed in bib-
liometric network studies [7,12].
From a software perspective (Figs. 1 and 2), the Shiny-based
implementation supports multiple input formats and generates export-
able visual outputs, including network diagrams, SSplots [7,12], Sankey
diagrams [6], Kano plots [25], and structured summary tables. The
browser-based workflow improves accessibility for users without
advanced programming expertise while supporting reproducible bib-
liometric analysis and visualization.
Nevertheless, several limitations should be noted. First, the top-N
filtering strategy may exclude low-frequency but potentially meaning-
ful nodes, which may affect detailed semantic interpretation. Second,
the leader–follower assumption used in FLCA may not fully capture
overlapping or non-hierarchical community structures [8–12]. Third,

5. Conclusion
ClusterChoice provides an efficient and interpretable framework for
bibliometric clustering. By combining top-N node filtering, FLCA-based
leader–follower clustering, and comparative quality metrics, it reduces
network complexity while improving cluster readability and evaluation
transparency. The results support ClusterChoice as a practical web-
based tool for selecting suitable clustering algorithms and generating
reproducible visual outputs for bibliometric and network analysis.
